newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Movies struggle to make Shakespeare accessible.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Movies struggle to make Shakespeare accessible.

text.p: The Capulets and Montagues are rival gangs in "Verona Beach" -- a city in an imaginary Latin American country. Cruising custom-made cars, ghetto blasters booming, they pop drugs in search of the next party.

Romeo's gang wear Hawaiian shirts and sport punky dyed hair. The Capulets are Latino types wearing slick Italian designer gear. The priest, who secretly marries the "star-crossed lovers", is a tattooed hippy who mixes dubious herbal potions.
William Shakespeare's "Romeo and Juliet" is the latest film based on the bard's plays that goes to inspired lengths to make his 16th century work accessible to a modern audience.
Its MTV-style fast editing and pulsating soundtrack are a far cry from the period costumes and received pronunciation English often associated with Shakespeare productions.
But of all Shakespeare film adaptations, it is the biggest box-office hit ever and its makers tout it as "the kind of film Shakespeare would like to have made".

After its international premiere at the Berlin film festival, director Baz Luhrmann, who also made "Strictly Ballroom" that was feted at the Cannes film festival in 1994, argued his approach was in the true spirit of Shakespeare.
"Shakespeare would do anything to communicate his stories," Australian Luhrmann told a news conference after the screening at Europe's second most important film festival after Cannes.
"The key for us was that when the guy wrote these plays they were for everyone. Our interest was to claim them back for that audience," he said of the U.S-Australian co-production.

"Convincing studios to take up the idea was a great struggle. When it became number one in the U.S. it was a great surprise," he said of the $20 million-budget film that grossed $65 million in the United States and Canada in a few months.
DIFFICULTY IN MAKING SHAKESPEARE ACCESSIBLE
Past film versions of Shakespeare plays often only get as far as small art-house audiences or win wider audiences as traditional costume dramas with well-known Hollywood stars.
Luhrmann argued he had found a simple recipe for success: "Unlike past Shakespeare film versions I didn't change the words -- I just cut them by about a third, to keep the pace."

But he admitted that the 16th century English, often complex poetry in archaic forms of verse, had required a special method for the predominantly U.S. cast -- many of whom felt they were grappling with a foreign language.
"Shakespeare can be obscure. It's another language," said 17-year-old starlet Claire Danes, who played Juliet.
Danes said Luhrmann had forced her and the other actors to do "ridiculous" exercises in which they had to describe each word with their bodies until they understand what it meant.
"Juliet is just a chick, a girl who a lot of dramatic things happen to in a short space of time," Danes said of her role.

No matter how obscure the plays may seem today -- with abundant references to classical mythology or ancient history and the difficult language -- directors and actors seem determined not to let them become extinct.
RECENT FLURRY OF SHAKESPEARE FILMS

If a recent flurry of film productions is anything to go by, Shakespeare's work is very much alive 400 years on as film directors compete to find more and more innovative or sensational ways to make it accessible to the masses.
Luhrmann's version of the famous love story coincides with the 400-year anniversary of the publication of Shakespeare's text of "Romeo and Juliet" in 1597.

It also comes in the wake of another film version that came out last year: "Tromeo and Juliet", set in downtown Manhattan among sleazy rival gangs of punks, which has been panned by critics as infantile and tasteless.
Critics acclaimed Hollywood star Al Pacino's recent documentary film called "Looking for Richard", which tries to explain Shakespeare's historical play "Richard III" to a contemporary audience.

British actor Kenneth Branagh, who has masterminded screen versions of several Shakespeare plays, has just produced a four-hour film of "Hamlet" and British director Trevor Nunn -- a new film production of "Twelfth Night".
Pacino addresses the problems modern audiences face by explaining the 16th century language and references which are no longer common knowledge.
Twentieth Century Fox, which produced both Luhrmann's and Pacino's films, has launched an initiative in Germany to show them in 10,000 schools across the country.

The project is called "A new look at Shakespeare" and is run jointly with German foundation Lesen, which promotes reading skills. Children will be given information packs about the plays and films with suggestions on new ways of reading them.
One million copies of a literary quiz called "Romeo and Juliet" will be distributed to thousands of German bookshops and libraries when the film goes on general release in March.
"In this way we hope to awaken an interest among young people in films and books," Fox and Lesen said in a statement.

Other new Shakespeare films are unlikely to qualify for inclusion in educational programmes. "Tromeo and Juliet" depicts body piercing, bestiality and the vomiting of colourful substances while the text is a string of expletives which critics have argued has little to do with Shakespeare at all.
Romeo proposes to Juliet while seated on a toilet and his reply to her words "Parting is such sweet sorrow", in the famous balcony scene is: "It sucks".

Purists might argue that such renditions are sacrilege. But even Shakespeare devotees agree theatre or drama is a living form and it is not only in this century that directors have adapted Shakespeare's works according to the spirit of the times.
In Shakespeare's day female roles were played by men and in the 19th century tragedies were re-written with happy endings.
